reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A Killian-Jamieson diverticulum is a pulsion outpouching that herniates through the Killian-Jamieson space, an anterolateral muscular gap in the proximal cervical oesophagus just below the cricopharyngeus and lateral to the longitudinal muscle insertion.
It is much less common than a Zenker diverticulum and arises below rather than above the cricopharyngeus, which is the key anatomical distinction.
On barium swallow it projects anterolaterally (more often on the left) below the upper oesophageal sphincter, whereas a Zenker diverticulum arises posteriorly above the sphincter.
Most are small and asymptomatic; larger ones may cause dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, cough or a palpable neck fullness.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in close relationship to the diverticular neck, so surgical or endoscopic treatment carries a real risk of vocal cord palsy.

Because of the nerve relationship, endoscopic septotomy (as used for Zenker) is generally avoided or approached with great caution, and open transcervical diverticulectomy is often preferred for symptomatic lesions.
It may be discovered incidentally during thyroid ultrasound as a cystic or mixed lesion abutting the thyroid, and can be mistaken for a thyroid nodule.
Cricopharyngeal dysfunction and raised intraluminal pressure are thought to contribute, so myotomy considerations may apply as in other pulsion diverticula.
reference.pathophysiology: The Killian-Jamieson diverticulum is a pulsion (false) diverticulum containing mucosa and submucosa but lacking a muscular wall, herniating through the Killian-Jamieson triangle. This is a muscular weak point in the anterolateral wall of the proximal cervical oesophagus, bounded by the oblique fibres of the cricopharyngeus superiorly and the longitudinal and circular muscle of the oesophagus, located just distal to the cricopharyngeus and inferior to the recurrent laryngeal nerve entry. Elevated intraluminal pressure, often related to incoordination or spasm of the upper oesophageal sphincter and cricopharyngeal dysfunction, drives mucosal herniation through this defect. Because the sac lies below the sphincter and adjacent to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, it differs anatomically and surgically from the posteriorly located, supra-sphincteric Zenker diverticulum.
additionalDifferentials: thyroid nodule or cyst on imaging
additionalInvestigations: barium swallow with lateral and oblique cervical views to define sac position relative to the cricopharyngeus
upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to inspect the ostium and exclude mucosal disease
neck ultrasound, which may first detect the lesion adjacent to the thyroid
cross-sectional imaging (computed tomography of the neck) to clarify anatomy before intervention
high-resolution manometry to assess upper sphincter function
laryngoscopic assessment of vocal cord function before any planned surgery
redFlags: new hoarseness or vocal cord palsy indicating recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement
signs of perforation such as neck pain, crepitus or fever after instrumentation
reference.prognosis: Small asymptomatic diverticula have an excellent prognosis and can be observed, while symptomatic lesions generally respond well to surgical diverticulectomy. The principal prognostic concern is iatrogenic recurrent laryngeal nerve injury during treatment.
pitfalls: Misidentifying the sac as a thyroid nodule on ultrasound and subjecting it to inappropriate biopsy.
Applying a standard endoscopic Zenker septotomy and injuring the adjacent recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Confusing it with a Zenker diverticulum because the anatomical distinction below versus above the cricopharyngeus is not appreciated.
Attempting fine-needle aspiration of a presumed thyroid lesion and causing perforation or infection.
Overlooking coexisting cricopharyngeal dysfunction that may need to be addressed.
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease, current edition
Shackelford's Surgery of the Alimentary Tract, current edition
management: Conservative observation for small, incidental, asymptomatic diverticula
Dietary and postural measures for mild symptoms, including thorough chewing, an upright posture at meals and avoiding food before lying down
Open transcervical diverticulectomy as the preferred definitive treatment for symptomatic lesions, given the intimate relation to the recurrent laryngeal nerve
Avoid or approach with great caution endoscopic septotomy, which carries a high risk of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury in this location, unlike for a Zenker diverticulum
High-resolution manometry to assess upper oesophageal sphincter dysfunction, with cricopharyngeal myotomy considered where indicated
Pre-operative laryngoscopic assessment of vocal cord function and post-operative monitoring for vocal cord palsy
Multidisciplinary ENT and upper gastrointestinal surgical input for planning intervention
